sense: a bird of the burning ground

note: Patitruppattu 11 likens the Chera, who reached the sea and felled the enemy's guarded kadamba at the root (முழுமுதல் துமிய), to Murugan who cut down Sur at the root (சூருடை முழுமுதல் தடிந்த); Thirumurugatruppadai 45-60 tells the god's deed itself: he entered the cold sea and cut Sur at the root (சூர்முதல் தடிந்த), the mango at its trunk.
teaches: Thirumurugatruppadai shows that cutting the root in the sea was already the god's signature deed, so the Chera poet's repeated phrase is a claim that the king's sea raid re-enacted Murugan's myth, with the enemy's guardian tree standing in for Sur's tree.

note: Kural 734 defines a land as one free of crushing hunger, unceasing disease and destructive foes; Patitruppattu 13 ends that the land the king guards has flowered, rid of disease and hunger (நோயொடு பசி இகந்து), after showing the enemy lands he ruined.
teaches: The Kural states the absences that make a land; the Chera poem shows who secures them and at whose cost, since the same king's anger is the destructive foe of his neighbours, so the definition is met at home by being broken next door.

note: Purananuru 117 says Pari's land kept its rain even when Venus ran to the south and other evil signs appeared; Patitruppattu 13 says that in the king's guarded land Venus does not run into the burning quarter and rain stands where it is wanted.
teaches: Read together, the two show two views of the omen: the lament makes a just ruler's land immune to the bad sign, while the Chera praise has the good ruler prevent the sign itself, so royal virtue was imagined as reaching even the planets' course.

note: Purananuru 2 likens Udhiyan Cheralathan's patience, counsel, strength, wrath and grace to the five great elements; Patitruppattu 14 tells his son, named in the decade's preface as Udhiyan Cheral's son, that he is as beyond measure as earth, water, wind and sky.
teaches: Father and son are both praised through the elements, which shows the element catalogue working as a Chera family formula, and the son's version moves the point from the elements' separate qualities to their shared immeasurability.

note: Purananuru 20 says that even if one could measure the sea's depth, the earth's breadth, the wind's paths and the sky, the Chera's knowledge, compassion and kindness could not be measured; Patitruppattu 14 says the king is as immeasurable as earth, water, wind and sky.
teaches: One poet makes the elements measurable so that the king can exceed them, the other makes them the standard of the unmeasurable, which shows that the same four-part catalogue could rank a king either above nature or alongside it.

note: Both are reports of having seen the enemy's ruined land (கண்டனென் in Purananuru 23, கண்டுவந் திசினே in Patitruppattu 15), and both mark the ruin by white velai flowers growing over it (வேளை வெண்பூ; வெண்பூ வேளை).
teaches: The shared white velai shows it was a stock sign of a razed settlement in both Pandya and Chera praise, and Patitruppattu 15 extends the form: where Purananuru 23 ends on the waste, the Chera poet adds a second sight, the king's own guarded land, so the ruin becomes one half of a judgment on rule.

note: The same line, எழுமுடி கெழீஇய திருஞெமர் அகலத்து, describes the king's chest in 14 line 11, where it is the shield of the worthy, and in 16 line 17, where it is the queen's longed-for bed.
teaches: The decade reuses one formula of the crowned chest for war and for love, so the turn in 16 to the waiting queen is built from the same praise language and makes the protector of the realm the cause of her loneliness.
audit_text_issue: Patitruppattu 16 lines 14 and 18-19 are obscure.

note: 16 asks whether the queen's bed will escape loneliness while the king lingers in camp; 19 says his love of war leaves no grace even for his modest wife, who has him only in dreams on the rare night he sleeps.
teaches: Taken together, the two poems show the decade returning to the queen's cost of war as a counter-voice inside praise, and 19 sharpens the question of 16 into a charge, set beside the ruin of the enemy's farmers.
audit_text_issue: Lines 9-15 of 19 and 14, 18-19 of 16 are hard to construe; the readings of the queen's lines are tentative.

note: Patitruppattu 17 says the king's great victory drum was made from the kadamba he cut after driving back the sea (கடம்பு அறுத்து இயற்றிய வலம்படு வியன்பணை); in Akananuru 347 the heroine compares the street's gossip to the drum of Cheralathan who drove back the sea and cut the kadamba (கடம்பு அறுத்து இயற்றிய பண்ணமை முரசின்).
teaches: The near-identical wording shows an akam poet borrowing the Chera's victory drum, a puram fact, to measure how loud gossip is, so the king's war trophy had become familiar enough to serve as a household simile for noise.

note: Kural 211 makes the rain the model of giving that seeks no return; Patitruppattu 18 says that even if the rain-cloud fails for many years, Cheralathan will not fail the bards' hope.
teaches: The Kural treats rain as the standard for duty-bound giving, but the Chera poem ranks the king above that standard because rain can fail, so the bards' praise claims for a patron a reliability the ethics book grants only to nature.

note: Both close on the failure of rain: 18 says Cheralathan will not lie even if rain fails for many years (மன்உயிர் அழிய யாண்டுபல துளக்கி ... தண்இயல் எழிலி தலையாது மாறி); 20 repeats the lines for the drought (மன்உயிர் அழிய யாண்டுபல மாறித் தண்இயல் எழிலி தலையா(து) ஆயினும்) and adds that he will not let a belly go hungry.
teaches: The repeated lines show that the decade has a fixed formula for drought, and 20 turns the general promise of 18 into a concrete guarantee against hunger, ending in a blessing on the mother who bore the giver.

note: The preface says the king carved his bow on the Himalaya and brought costly vessels with diamonds (அருவிலை நன்கலம் வயிரமொடு கொண்டு) to his old city and gave to others; Akananuru 127 recalls Cheralathan who drove off the sea, cut the kadamba, carved his bow on the Himalaya and heaped the foes' tribute of fine vessels with diamonds (நன்கலம் ... வயிரமொடு) at Maanthai, leaving it for the earth to eat.
teaches: The two record the same hoard with the same jewel list but different fates, given away in the preface and left buried in the akam poem, so an akam poet could cite a puram event precisely while turning its moral from royal giving to abandoned wealth, the wealth the lover will not linger for.

note: Kural 86 says the one who tends the departing guest and watches for the next becomes a good guest of those in the sky; Patitruppattu 21 calls the king's kitchen-fat an ஆவுதி (oblation) beside the sacrificial one and says the two smells together please the gods who abide in the sky.
teaches: The Chera poem shows the mechanism the Kural only asserts: feeding guests reaches the gods because the kitchen smoke is itself counted as an oblation, so hospitality was understood as a second sacrifice rather than merely compared to one.

note: Kural 578 gives the world to those able to show kannottam without spoiling the task; Patitruppattu 22 lists கழிகண்ணோட்டம், excessive kindly regard, among the obstacles to the wheel of dharma, beside anger and harsh punishment.
teaches: The Chera list names as a fault exactly the excess the Kural's condition guards against, which shows that the Kural's praise of kannottam was already bounded in older court ethics where too much mercy blocked a king's justice.

note: Kural 567 says harsh words and punishment beyond bounds are a file that wears down a king's power; Patitruppattu 22 puts தெறல் கடுமை, severity of punishment, in one list with too much kindness and too much love as obstacles to dharma's wheel.
teaches: Read together, the Kural treats harshness on its own while the Chera poem sets it beside its opposite excesses, so the older list frames royal justice as a mean between cruelty and indulgence rather than as the avoidance of cruelty alone.

note: In Purananuru 23 the poet says he has come having seen Nedunchezhiyan's work in enemy land, which ends as a waste where a doe whose stag a tiger killed nibbles velai with her fawn; in Patitruppattu 23 the bards say they came and saw (கண்டனம்) the lands of the Chera's foes turned to forest where the wild cow lives happily with her bull.
teaches: The two bards' reports end on a female beast in the ruined land, but Kalladanar's widowed doe carries the human loss into the forest while Gauthamanar's paired wild cow celebrates the wilderness's return, so the same reporting convention could either mourn or exult over conquest.

note: Kural 560 says that if the guardian does not guard, the cows' yield fails and those of the six duties forget their books; Patitruppattu 24 names the six duties (ஓதல் வேட்டல் அவைபிறர்ச் செய்தல் ஈதல் ஏற்றல்) and says the king walks by the word of those who keep them, so that the world walks by his.
teaches: The Kural makes the Brahmins' learning depend on the king's protection, while the Chera poem makes the king's conduct depend on the Brahmins' word, so the pair shows the relation running both ways: guarded by the king, they in turn guide him.

note: Kural 559 says if the king bends justice the sky withholds its rain; Patitruppattu 24 ends that even if the rain-cloud forgets its season the king's wealth will keep its yield.
teaches: The Kural binds the land's rain to the king's justice, but the praise poem claims the just king's plenty survives even a failed monsoon, so court praise pushed royal power past the cosmic dependence the ethical maxim keeps.

note: Purananuru 25 asks whether Chezhiyan's spear stopped short of further ruin when he saw the widows beating their breasts and cutting their hair; in Patitruppattu 26 the poet himself says நோகோ யானே, I grieve, at the enemy land the Chera's warriors ravaged, whose people blame the season.
teaches: Held together, the two show that pity for the conquered had a place inside victory praise in two forms, as the king's hoped-for restraint in the Pandya poem and as the poet's own grief in the Chera one, and in neither as blame of the king.

note: Patitruppattu 27 describes the enemy's watered land, ruined by the king's angry look, as knowing no uproar but the carters' shouting; 28 says the king's own land knows no heat but the uproar of the river's red flood.
teaches: The poet uses the same 'no uproar but a harmless one' figure for the land the king destroys and the land he guards, which shows that the two were equally blessed and that only the king's anger made the difference.

note: Purananuru 20 tells a Chera that those in his shade know no burning but the cooking fire and the sun, no bow but the rainbow and no weapon but the plough; Patitruppattu 28 says the Chera's land knows no heat but the uproar of the great river's flood, even in drought.
teaches: Both Chera poems praise the guarded land by negating violence with a harmless counterpart, and the Patitruppattu adds that the protection holds in drought because the river floods when the hills are dry, so the figure served as a court convention that each poet bent to a new claim.
audit_text_issue: Patitruppattu 28 line 6 (நீணதொழில்) looks corrupt.

note: Patitruppattu 23 shows the king feeding the street-singing bards (வயிரிய மாக்கள் ... மறுகுசிறை பாடும்) even in a drought; 29 uses the same line-words for bards tuning lutes and singing at street corners in the enemy's settlements before the army spread.
teaches: The singing bard is the decade's sign of a living land, so 29 measures the enemy's loss by the very figure 23 uses for the king's bounty: the war silences in other lands the music the king pays for at home.

note: Purananuru 2 praises Udhiyan Cheralathan, called பெருஞ்சோற்று in his colophon name, for giving the great rice without limit while the hundred fought the five; Patitruppattu 30, colophon பெருஞ்சோற்றுநிலை, sung for a son of that line, shows the rite: the drum calls warriors to scatter the great rice, a blood-mixed ball offered to the god and eaten by crows and kites.
teaches: The father's poem only names the great rice as a gift of food, while the son's shows it as a pre-battle offering that binds the warriors and frightens the enemy, so the pair shows the perunjoru as a Chera rite of war that the Purananuru's epithet assumed.
audit_text_issue: Line 6 is a repaired reading.

note: Patitruppattu 24 praises the king for walking by the word of the Brahmins who keep the six duties; the preface of the decade says he made the elders of moon-clear tradition his own and finally went to the forest with Nedumbarathayanar leading.
teaches: The preface completes the portrait of 24: the king whose rule followed the learned Brahmins ended by following one of them out of rule into the forest, so the deference the song praises was remembered as leading to renunciation.

note: Kural 301 says anger is truly restrained only where it could take effect; Patitruppattu 32 marvels that the king, having broken the enemy and taken their land, is not angry even in the country of those who reviled him.
teaches: The Kural's rule names the only test of restraint that counts, and the Chera poem shows a king passing it at the one moment conquest gives his anger full power, which is why the poet calls it a wonder rather than a duty.

note: Kural 750 says that whatever excellences a fort has, it is nothing without men excellent in action; Patitruppattu 33 makes the marching army itself a fortress, swords for wall, spears for hedge and arrows for moat.
teaches: The Kural makes the defenders the real worth of a fort, and the Chera poet takes that to its end by removing the walls altogether, so that the fort exists wherever the army camps.

note: Purananuru 62 asks what winning a war can mean when both kings die, and shows demon women dancing in the blood of the dead; Patitruppattu 35 shows demons dancing in the red field and calls that war the king's unfailing wealth.
teaches: The same picture of demons dancing on the blood-field is proof of glory when a victor lives to be praised and proof of futility when no one is left to take the field, so the image itself carries no verdict and the surviving king supplies it.

note: Purananuru 369, a kalavazhi for another Chera, maps the battle onto rain and tillage, with elephants as clouds and chariots as ploughs; Patitruppattu 36, also kalavazhi, has the elephants fall with trunks cut like palms in a cleared field.
teaches: Read together, the two show the kalavazhi of the Chera court treating slaughter as farm work, a single cleared-field simile in one poem and a full season of ploughing and harvest in the other, so the thurai's name from the threshing floor shapes its images.

note: Kural 546 says victory comes not from the spear but from the sceptre that does not bend; Patitruppattu 37 lists the king's victory (வலம்படு வென்றியும்) and his unbending principle (கோடாக் கொள்கையும்) as two separate things he has.
teaches: The Kural makes straight rule the cause of victory, while the Chera poet sets the two side by side as distinct possessions, so the praise poem lacks the causal claim the maxim adds and shows the two were first counted as separate royal goods.

note: Kural 322 ranks sharing food (பகுத்துண்டு) first among all that the authors gathered (தொகுத்தவற்றுள்); Patitruppattu 38 praises the king for the manliness that gathered the sharing of food (பகுத்(து)ஊண் தொகுத்த ஆண்மை) and for living for others.
teaches: The same pair of words, sharing and gathering, ranks a virtue in the Kural's list of teachings and names a king's acquired valour in the Chera poem, so a virtue the Kural places among the vows against killing appears here as a warrior's manhood.

note: Purananuru 182 says the world endures because there are people who will not eat even nectar alone and who strive for others, not for themselves; Patitruppattu 38 says the king has no wish to enjoy sweet things alone and lives for others.
teaches: The Purananuru gives an unnamed class of people on whom the world rests, and the Chera praise gives the same refusal to eat alone to one named king, which shows the court poet drawing on a general moral picture to make the patron its single instance.

note: Akananuru 199 measures the wealth a man refuses to leave his wife for by the land Narmudi Cheral regained when Nannan fell in the battle at the great ford of the vakai; Patitruppattu 40 praises the same Narmudi Cheral for cutting down Nannan's vakai at the root.
teaches: The love poem adds that the country won from Nannan was one the Chera had lost before (இழந்த நாடு), which the praise poem does not say, and it shows the king's greatest gain already serving akam poets as the very largest wealth a lover could turn down.

note: Kuruntokai 73 says the Kosar killed Nannan's fragrant mango tree and drove him from his land; the preface of the fourth ten says Narmudi Cheral beheaded Nannan of Peruvaayil and felled his gold-bearing vakai.
teaches: On a plain reading the two disagree on which tree was Nannan's guardian and who destroyed him, so either the name Nannan covers more than one chief or felling his guarded tree was a victory several conquerors claimed, and neither poem alone shows that the deed was told of more than one enemy.

note: Kural 776 says the hero counts as wasted every day on which he took no noble wound; Patitruppattu 42 says the king's men wear the thumbai only beside men whose bodies already hold arrows and whose chests show the surgeon's needle-scars.
teaches: The Kural keeps the ledger of wounds inside one man's private reckoning, while the Chera poem turns it into a rule of the company, so that scars decide who may stand in the thumbai line and the wound becomes a public credential rather than a personal measure.

note: Kural 211 says duty seeks no return, as the world gives nothing back to the rain; Patitruppattu 43 likens the king's giving to rain that breaks a drought and floods the river banks.
teaches: Both take rain as the model of giving, but the Kural uses it to show giving without return, while the Chera poet uses drought-breaking rain to show giving measured by need and graded by receiver, so the same image yields a rule of disinterest in one and a rule of fit in the other.

note: Patitruppattu 11 says Nedum Cheralathan cut down the enemy's kadamba at the root and made of it his roaring war drum; Patitruppattu 44 says his son cut the Mohur king's neem at the root to make a drum and dragged it off with elephants.
teaches: Read together, the father's kadamba and the son's neem show the guardian tree turned into the victor's drum as a rite of the Chera line, repeated across generations, so that each king's voice in war is literally made from a defeated enemy's sacred tree.

note: Akananuru 347 measures the town's gossip by the drum of Cheralathan made from the kadamba he cut after driving back the sea; Patitruppattu 44 shows the making of such a drum from the Mohur neem.
teaches: The puram decade shows how a Chera trophy drum was made from a felled guardian tree, and the akam poem shows that drum so well known that a heroine can use its roar to measure the gossip about her, so a war trophy had passed into the household's common speech.

note: Patitruppattu 20 says Nedum Cheralathan went against foes on an island in the sea and cut their kadamba; Patitruppattu 45 says his son threw his spear and drove back the sea itself, which no rain or river can change.
teaches: Set side by side, the father's war against islanders in the sea and the son's spear thrown at the sea show the decade's title growing from a naval campaign into a feat against nature, with the human enemy dropped and the sea left as the only adversary worth naming.

note: Patitruppattu 47 says that whenever Kuttuvan slays, the suppliants never cease receiving elephants; in Purananuru 394 a bard given a killing elephant is terrified, sends it back, and is given a bigger one, so he warns other poets away.
teaches: On one reading the war elephant is the crown of royal gifts, and on the other it is a burden a poor bard cannot use or feed, so the pair shows the gift-poem's ideal of the elephant gift and the bard's comic protest against it from inside the same tradition.

note: Patitruppattu 44 gives the cause of the Mohur war, the king's pledge to the distant Arukai, and the felling of the neem; Patitruppattu 49 gives the kings and Velir who massed at Mohur, the blood-flood and the ruin.
teaches: The two songs divide one campaign between them, the reason and the trophy in one and the coalition and slaughter in the other, so the decade tells a single war across separate praise poems and needs both to be read as history.

note: Akananuru 214 has a soldier in the rain-soaked camp where the king, eager for glory, does not sleep, asking how his wife bears the evenings alone; Patitruppattu 50 asks how the sleepless king himself passes the camp days away from women's embrace.
teaches: The akam poem treats the king's sleeplessness as the cause of the soldier's separation, while the puram poet lends the king the soldier's own longing to praise his endurance, so the same camp night is a lover's grief in one book and a king's virtue in the other.
audit_text_issue: Patitruppattu 50 lines 8-10 are partly corrupt (மன்ண, வொணஇய).

note: Patitruppattu 44 says the king cut the Mohur neem at the root and dragged it with elephants for a drum; the preface names it as the neem guarded by Pazhaiyan and says the elephant cart was tied with ropes of his widowed wives' hair.
teaches: The preface supplies the detail the song withholds, the rope of the defeated king's widows' hair, so the felling of the tree is shown to be a humiliation of the enemy's household as well as the taking of his sacred tree.

note: Kural 222 says taking is bad even if called a good path, and giving good even without a higher world; Patitruppattu 52 says the king's hand bends down to give to suppliants and does not know how to open upward to take (இரப்போர்க்குக் கவிதல் அல்லதை இரைஇய மலர்பு அறியா).
teaches: The poem turns the couplet's two verbs into two postures of one hand, palm down to give and palm up to receive, so the rule against taking becomes a bodily habit the king cannot break.

note: In Purananuru 98 the foes who see Anji's war elephants with blunted tusks bar their fort gates; Patitruppattu 53 warns the Chera to take another road home, since his elephant, seeing any gate, will charge it.
teaches: Read together they show the praise of the war elephant pushed one step further: in Avvai's poem the gates close in fear, while the Chera poet makes the elephant's habit so fixed that the king's own ancestral city is in danger, so the boast works by turning the threat inward.

note: Kural 222 says giving is good even if there were no higher world; Patitruppattu 54 wishes that the giving king not go to the high world (உயர்நிலை உலகத்துச் செல்லாது) but stay long on the earth.
teaches: The couplet sets heaven aside as irrelevant to the worth of giving, while the bard treats the giver's heaven as a loss to those who live on his gifts and wishes it postponed, so the same detachment of giving from heaven appears once as an ethic and once as the suppliants' self-interest.

note: Kural 211 asks what the world gives back to the rain, to show that obligation seeks no return; Patitruppattu 55 wishes the giving king's days to pass like white clouds that pour rain, protect the land and go up to rest on the hill.
teaches: Both use the rain cloud for the giver, but the Kural stops at the absence of return, while the Chera poem imagines what the cloud has after giving, rest on the hill, and makes that the blessing on the king's lifespan.

note: Patitruppattu 56 says the king is not skilled at dancing before the drums of the festival ground (ஆடல் வல்லான் அல்லன்); 52, in the same decade, shows him leading the thunangai dance by lamplight, giving his lead hand, until the queen grows angry.
teaches: On a literal reading the two poems disagree about whether he dances at festivals, and holding them together shows that 56's denial is a joke the decade's hearers would see through, a mock dispraise that only works because his festival dancing was known.

note: Both are virali-guide poems that open with the same words, செல்லா மோதில் சில்வளை விறலி, and send the dancing woman to a king on the battlefield; Purananuru 64 says they will see Kudumi and leave behind their watery gruel, Patitruppattu 57 says they will see the king who fears suppliants' distress more than women's sulking eyes.
teaches: The shared formula shows that the virali guide poem had a fixed opening used across Pandya and Chera praise, and the difference in what follows shifts the motive from the bard's hunger in the Purananuru to the patron's own anxiety in the Patitruppattu.

note: Kural 224 says being begged from is painful until one sees the asker's glad face; Patitruppattu 57 says the king fears the distress of suppliants more than the sulking eyes of the women of his house (ஒண்நுதல் மகளிர் துனித்த கண்ணினும் இரவலர் புன்கண் அஞ்சும்).
teaches: The couplet names the giver's discomfort in general, and the poem measures it against the strongest private disturbance of akam, a wife's sulk, so the giver's pain is ranked above domestic love.

note: Kural 120 says true trade for merchants is caring for others' goods as their own; Patitruppattu 59 tells the king that protecting the land, where goods of hill and sea are shared out and the roads stay unblocked in the way of dharma, is his duty.
teaches: The Kural places fair trade in the merchant's conscience, while the Chera poem names the condition it assumes, open roads that the king must keep, so the trader's ethic depends on a ruler's duty the couplet does not mention.

note: Purananuru 236 is Kapilar's lament that Pari told him to stay behind and did not take him in death; Patitruppattu 61 has Kapilar, Pari gone to the land from which none returns (வாராச் சேண்புலம் படர்ந்தோன்), arrive at the Chera's camp drawn by a fame for giving without regret.
teaches: Together they show the bard's two answers to his patron's death, the vow to be with Pari in the next birth and the journey to a new patron whose giving is praised in Pari's terms, so the Chera's praise is partly an elegy carried over.

note: Patitruppattu 13 sets enemy farmland ruined by the king beside his own flowering land; Patitruppattu 62 describes a rich farm of cattle, grain heaps and toddy-drinking workers as what the enemy keeps if he bows and pays tribute.
teaches: The second decade shows ruin and plenty as two places; Kapilar makes them two futures of the same enemy land, so the farm scene becomes the terms of surrender rather than a picture of the king's own country.

note: Purananuru 3 tells the Pandya his word will not move even if the earth moves (நிலம் பெயரினும், நின்சொற் பெயரல்) and is husband of a lady of faultless chastity; Patitruppattu 63 tells the Chera that even when the earth changes its nature his spoken word does not fail.
teaches: The same hyperbole for a Pandya and a Chera shows that the unmoving royal word was shared praise across dynasties, and the Purananuru poet turns it into a lever (so read the suppliant's need) where Kapilar leaves it as one of four bounded traits.

note: In Purananuru 107 Kapilar says Pari is not the only one who sustains the world: there is also the rain; in Patitruppattu 64 the same poet tells the Chera that he pours greater benefit than the high cloud (மழையினும் பெரும்பயம் பொழிதி).
teaches: Kapilar's measure of a giver is the rain in both poems, but where Pari was granted only the rain as his equal the living Chera is set above it, which shows how the poet's praise scale shifted with the patron and how far the dead friend's standard was raised to honour the new one.

note: In Purananuru 105 Kapilar sends a singing woman to Pari, promising jewels for his gentleness, which is sweeter than the water falling on his hill; in Patitruppattu 67 he sends a bard to the Chera, promising pearls, and fills the road with the king's battlefield of vultures, demons and hacked bodies.
teaches: The same poet's two guide poems show that the guide form takes its content from the patron: a hill chief is reached through his kindness and his streams, a crowned king through the terror of his wars, though both end in the same gift of jewels.

note: Akananuru 61 tells the heroine not to suffer looking at the tall wall where the days are marked (நாள்இழை நெடுஞ்சுவர்), and pictures Pulli's men trading white elephant tusks for toddy; Patitruppattu 68 has the king's warriors hoping to trade white tusks (வெண்கோடு) for toddy while women at home draw the days on the painted wall.
teaches: The tusk bartered for toddy and the days scored on a wall were a stock pair of the far campaign and the waiting house: the akam poet splits them between the land the hero crosses and the heroine's room, while Kapilar keeps both inside one king's war, so the cost of conquest is counted at home.

note: Patitruppattu 16 asks whether the queen's bed will escape its loneliness while the king lingers in camp; Patitruppattu 68 shows women in the palace marking the days on the wall while the warriors fast before the fort.
teaches: Two poets of two decades both end a war poem at the women left behind, which shows the waiting house was a set part of Chera praise, and Kapilar extends it from the queen alone to the whole palace and sets the warriors' own longings beside it.

note: Patitruppattu 13 says that in the king's guarded land Venus does not run to the burning quarter and rain stands where wanted; Patitruppattu 69 says that under the rulers before him the land yielded, the sun's heat softened, Venus stood in its place and the rains answered need.
teaches: The second decade grants the good omens to the reigning king, while Kapilar grants them to the ancestors who were like him, so the same signs serve as proof of a present reign and as the inheritance a king must live up to.

note: Kural 43 makes the chief duty the care of five: ancestors, gods, guests, kin and oneself; Patitruppattu 70 says the king, with his kin around him, fed the gods with sacrifice, pleased the sages with learning, put elders before his sons, and so paid the ancient debts (தொல்கடன்).
teaches: Read together, they show two accounts of what a man owes: the Kural spreads the duty over five equal claims including guests and himself, while the Chera poem counts it as an inherited debt to gods, sages and elders paid off by sacrifice and learning, so the king's virtue is framed as settlement rather than care.

note: Purananuru 5 tells a Chera, lord of a forest land where elephants spread like cattle, to keep away from those who cast off grace and love and to guard the realm as one rears a child; Patitruppattu 71 shows the king burning towns and taking cattle and tribute, then says that had he not weighed the strong and the simple and shown grace (அருளாய் ஆயின்), no one here would live.
teaches: Purananuru 5 asks for grace as the standing temper of a ruler's guard, while Patitruppattu 71 finds it only after conquest, as the sparing of the defeated who pay tribute, so the two Chera poems show grace counselled as a principle of rule and praised as a victor's restraint.

note: Akananuru 135 likens the heroine's shaken heart to Kazhuvul's Kamur when fourteen Velir attacked it together; Patitruppattu 71 has Kazhuvul, chief of those who live by cattle, bow his head (கழுவுள் தலைமடங்க) when the Chera's archers drove off the herds.
teaches: Kazhuvul is besieged by a coalition of Velir in one poem and humbled by the Chera in the other, which shows his herders' stronghold as a repeated prey of greater powers and explains why an akam poet could use it as a byword for a heart under assault.

note: 71 line 25 has the king weigh the strong and the simple (உரவரும் மடவரும் அறிவுதெரிந்(து) எண்ணி) before he shows grace; 73 line 1 has the strong and the simple reckon the king (உரவோர் எண்ணினும் மடவோர் எண்ணினும்) and find no one to compare him to.
teaches: The decade turns the same pair round: first the king judges the wise and the foolish to decide whom to spare, then the wise and the foolish judge him and find no measure, so judgement runs both ways between the king and those he rules.

note: Kural 467 says to think and then resolve, and that to think after resolving is a lapse; Patitruppattu 72 says the king's foes, from the greatness of their enmity and their folly, resolve without deliberating (சூழாது துணிதல்), unlike the wise who know his nature, and meet him as the doom-fire.
teaches: The Kural gives the rule as prudence in any task, while the Chera poem applies it to war and shows its breach as ruin, setting the wise counsellors who know the king against the foes who resolve unthinking, so deliberation becomes the line between the king's servants and his victims.

note: Kural 7 says the mind's anxiety is hard to remove except for those who reach the feet of the one who has no comparison; Patitruppattu 73 calls the Chera one to whom others are no comparison (நினக்குப் பிறர்உவமம் ஆகா) and ends with the poet grieving (வருந்துவல் யானே) that people will not believe his praise.
teaches: The Kural makes the incomparable one the end of anxiety for those who come to him, but the Chera poet shows the same attribute, given to a king, bringing anxiety to the one who praises, since what has no comparison cannot be made credible to hearers.
audit_text_issue: two lines lost after line 3

note: Kural 265 says tapas is striven for here because whatever is wanted is gained as it is wanted; Patitruppattu 74 says the king told his grey-haired elder that generosity, dignity, wealth, offspring, the divine and everything belong to those who have tapas (தவம்உடை யோர்க்கென), and let him go to the wide forest.
teaches: The Kural states the promise of tapas as a reason to strive, while the Chera poem shows a king applying it to another, releasing his aged counsellor from court to the forest, so tapas appears as the last stage of a life of royal service and its grant as a king's virtue.

note: 77 likens the Chera's many elephants to the cattle of the Kongar spreading over the gravel upland (கொங்கர் ஆபரந் தன்ன); 78 likens the horses and elephants he had in his own land after razing Tagadur to spreading goats and cattle (ஆபரந் தன்ன யானையோன்).
teaches: The decade moves the herd simile from the enemy's ground to the king's: first the elephants spread like a hostile people's cattle in an army on the march, then like home herds after victory, so one image marks war-strength turning into the settled wealth of peace.

note: Kural 443 says that to cherish the great and make them one's own is the rarest of rare things; Patitruppattu 79 says the king honours the great and cherishes the small (பெரியோர்ப் பேணிச் சிறியோரை அளித்தி), between lines on not sparing his life in war and sparing nothing in giving.
teaches: The Kural singles out honouring the great as a ruler's hardest gain, while the Chera poem pairs it with care for the small and sets both beside courage and giving, so the maxim appears as one term of a balanced royal portrait rather than a rarity standing alone.

note: The preface praises Perunjeral Irumporai for defeating Adhiyaman and razing Tagadur (தகடூர் எறிந்து), sung by Arisil Kizhar; Purananuru 230, by the same Arisil Kizhar, whose colophon names its subject as Ezhini the Adhiyaman who fell fighting at Tagadur, says Death lost more than the grieving, hungry world when it took him. On the reading that both refer to that war, one counts Tagadur's fall a glory and the other a loss to the whole world.
teaches: Read together, they show one court poet singing both sides of one war, the victor's fame and the fallen chief's elegy, so praise and lament were offices a poet filled by occasion, and the Tagadur campaign survives as triumph and as ruin in the same voice.

note: Akananuru 44 has a man bid his charioteer hurry home to his wife because the king's war is finished and the foes have paid tribute; Patitruppattu 81 has the poet ask the king himself, in the rainy season with the siege still on, to yoke his chariot for one day to see his wife, so that the sleepless besieged kings may sleep too (துஞ்சா வேந்தரும் துஞ்சுக).
teaches: In the akam poem the homecoming waits until the war is over, but the court poet asks the king to go home in the middle of the war and gives the besieged enemy's rest as a reason, so the mullai motif of the rainy-season return becomes, in praise poetry, a way of asking for a pause in the fighting.

note: 82 lines 12 and 13 praise wealth that does not lessen however much singers take and an army that does not lessen however much foes kill (கொளக்கொளக் குறையா, கொலக்கொலக் குறையா); 90 line 16 makes the same quality the ground of a likeness: like the sea, because taking does not diminish him (கொளக்குறை படாமையின் முந்நர்ண அனையை).
teaches: Read together, the two poems show the poet's own method of comparison: a quality he first states as a bare formula about wealth and army becomes, in the last poem of the decade, the stated reason why the king is like the sea, so the ground of the simile is set out before the simile is made.
audit_text_issue: Patitruppattu 90 line 16 prints முந்நர்ண for முந்நீர்.

note: 72 says the king's foes resolve without deliberating (சூழாது துணிதல்) and, from the greatness of their folly, do not know his nature as the wise do; 84 says his foes knew well that he was strong (வலியை ஆதல்நற்(கு) அறிந்தனர் ஆயினும்) and still rose against him, not knowing how to bow.
teaches: The two Chera decades give opposite causes for the same ruin: the eighth ten blames the enemy's ignorance of the king, the ninth blames their refusal to bow although they knew him, which moves the fault from a lack of judgement to pride.

note: In 61 Kapilar comes to the Chera after Pari's death, saying he will not beg or understate but has come for the king's fame for giving; 85 says this later Chera's gifts are more than the villages Kapilan won (கபிலன் பெற்ற ஊரினும் பலவே).
teaches: The seventh ten shows Kapilar arriving at the Chera court without a patron, and the ninth uses the reward he got there as the standard a later king's giving is said to exceed, so one poet's payment became the dynasty's own yardstick for generosity.

note: Purananuru 105 says Pari's gentleness is sweeter than the water that comes down every peak of his hill (நீரினும் இனிய சாயல்); Patitruppattu 86 says Poraiyan is sweeter and cooler of gentleness than the water of the Vaani (வானி நீரினும் தீந்தண் சாயலன்), after the poet admits he had feared him for his slaughter in war.
teaches: The formula of a patron gentler than running water passes from Kapilar's hill chief to a Chera king, but the later poet sets it against the king's reputation for bloodshed, so the same praise is used to answer a suppliant's fear of a warrior king.

note: Kural 386 says the land of a king easy to see and not harsh of speech is praised above others; Patitruppattu 86 tells how the report of the king's killing in war made the poet fear him, until he found him the patron of singers who ends the misery of the poor and is gentle as cool river water.
teaches: The couplet treats being easy to approach as a plain royal virtue, while the poem shows what it has to overcome: a king's fame for killing keeps suppliants away, so his accessibility has to be proved against his own reputation.

note: Purananuru 105 sends a bright-browed virali to Pari, saying she will get jewels (சேயிழை பெறுகுவை) and likening his gentleness to water coming down his hill; Patitruppattu 87 sends a singing woman to Poraiyan, saying she will get fine jewels (நன்கலம் பெறுகுவை) and setting his kindness against the cane carried by a flood that bears sandal to the sea.
teaches: Perunkunrur Kizhar splits Kapilar's single guide poem into two of his own, the water likeness in 86 and the sending of the singer with the promise of jewels in 87, which shows how a short Purananuru guide poem served the Patitruppattu poets as a pattern they could take apart.

note: The fourth preface tells Narmudi Cheral's own deed: he cut off Nannan's head and felled his gold-bearing vaakai at the root (பொன்படு வாகை முழுமுதல் தடிந்து); 88 lists the wearing down of Nannan of the bright-flowered vaakai (சுடர்வீ வாகை நன்னன் தேய்த்து) among the deeds of the ancestors (பெரியோர் மருக) of the ninth ten's king.
teaches: A victory that the fourth decade gives to one named king appears in the ninth as one item in a list of ancestral deeds, beside the kadamba and the spear thrown into the sea, so the decades show single kings' wars becoming the common record of the Chera line.

note: 20 answers 'who is your king?' with Neduncheralathan, who went against foes on an island of the sea and cut the kadamba at its root (கடம்புமுதல் தடிந்த); 88 has the kadamba's whole trunk felled and the spear hurled into the dark sea as deeds of the ancestors of the present king.
teaches: In the second ten the felling of the kadamba is what identifies one king to a stranger, and in the ninth it has become an inherited title that makes a later king great by descent, so the pair shows a personal feat hardening into a dynastic emblem.

note: Kural 545 says rain and harvest gather in the land of the king who rules by the right way; Patitruppattu 89 lists the rain in its season, the paired deer, the humming boughs, unfailing fruit and tubers, grazing herds and endless grain, then gives the cause: because your sceptre is straight (நின்கோல் செம்மையின்).
teaches: The couplet states the link between a just sceptre and rain as a rule, while the poem spreads its consequences over a whole countryside of herds, forest creatures and grain, which shows how wide a land's well-being the belief was taken to cover.

note: Purananuru 35 counsels the Chola that rain comes when sought in a land of the just sceptre and warns that if rain fails or yield shrinks the world blames its guardians (காவலர்ப் பழிக்கும்); Patitruppattu 89 tells the Chera that rain pours in season because his sceptre is straight and the land worships him daily.
teaches: The same belief works as praise in one poem and as warning in the other: credit for the rain in the Chera poem implies the blame for drought that the Chola poem spells out, so a king praised for good seasons was held answerable for bad ones.

note: Purananuru 2 says the Chera has forbearance, breadth of counsel, strength, fierceness and grace like the nature of the five elements, without saying which goes with which; Patitruppattu 90 likens the king to water for his kindness, to the sky for being beyond measure and to the sea for not lessening however much is taken, naming each ground.
teaches: The ninth ten does explicitly what the Purananuru catalogue leaves implicit, joining each natural power to one royal virtue by a stated reason, so the pair shows the elemental praise of Chera kings being turned from a list into reasoned comparison.
audit_text_issue: line 16 முந்நர்ண is a misprint for முந்நீர்

note: The seventh preface says Selvakkadungo, after his sacrifice, gave Ogandur and 'confounded the purohita' (புரோசு மயக்கி); the ninth preface uses the same phrase of Ilanjeral Irumporai (புரைஅறு கேள்விப் புரோசு மயக்கி), beside mantra worship, the installing of the spirits of the crossroads and the shanti rite.
teaches: The repeated phrase shows that the preface-writers had a fixed slot for a king's dealings with his purohita, and the ninth preface fills it with a larger ritual programme than the seventh, so the prefaces record the growing weight given to priestly rites in the picture of Chera kingship.

note: Fragment 1 says enemies cannot escape except by heaping rare jewels with elephants and speaking submissively (யானையொ(டு) அரும்கலம் ... பணிந்துவழி மொழிதல்); Akananuru 124 opens with the same formula (நன்கலம் களிற்றொடு ... வணங்கினர், வழிமொழிந்து) as the condition on which a soldier waiting in camp may go home to his wife.
teaches: The submission the praise poet demands as the enemy's only course is, in the akam poem, the event a homesick soldier waits for, so the formula of tribute served both genres and the end of the king's war was imagined from the camp as the start of a lover's return.
audit_text_issue: Fragment line 7 carries a repaired TSCII reading and the marker flagged the fragment's sense as uncertain.

note: Fragment 1 states as the poet's rhetorical question that enemies have no way but to submit (பணிந்துவழி மொழிதல் அல்லது); Purananuru 17 gives the enemy kings' own words as they decide to submit to the Chera Irumporai for fear of losing their walls and forts.
teaches: Held together, the two show that the Chera praise poets treated submission not only as the king's due but as a reasoned choice the enemy makes on seeing his anger, so the boast of the fragment rests on a scene of calculation that Purananuru 17 spells out.
audit_text_issue: Fragment 1 is a fragment and the marker flagged its sense.

note: Kural 744 says a fort is that which destroys the besieging enemy's spirit (உறுபகை ஊக்கம் அழிப்ப தரண்); Fragment 2 lists a fort with tall wall, battlements, guard forest and deep moat and says that it is the defending kings who lose heart (நெஞ்சுபுகல் அழிந்து) at the Chera march.
teaches: On the plain reading the two make opposite claims about the same contest of nerve: the Kural gives the fort the power to break the attacker's spirit, while the praise poem says a perfect fort could not keep its own kings' spirit from breaking, so the war of morale the Kural assigns to walls the poet assigns to the king's army.
audit_text_issue: Line 6 (ஊன்வினை கடுக்குந்) is obscure.

note: Fragment 3 has a woman say that another, for all her excellence, is not her equal and knows who her equals are (என்னொடு புரையுநள் அல்லள்); Ainkurunuru 67, a wife's speech in marutham, says the hero's new woman, foolish, sets herself against the wife who is no match for her (தன்னொடு நிகரா என்னொடு நிகரி).
teaches: Ainkurunuru 67 supplies the frame the three-line fragment lacks: claims of who is whose equal are the weapon of the marutham quarrel between wife and new woman, which makes it likely the fragment is such a speech and that its point is standing in the household rather than beauty.

note: Fragment 4 has the bard come to see the king (வந்தனென் பெரும கண்டனென்) in his camp with the army camped in foreign land (வேறுபுலத்(து) இறுத்த ... தானையொடு), where elephants full of strength (மைந்துமலி) tear up their posts; Purananuru 22 ends with the poet come to see the Chera Irumporai (வந்து இனிது காண்டிசின்) with his army camping in foreign land (வேறுபுலத்து இறுக்கும் தானையோடு) and opens with strong elephants (மைந்து மலிந்த மழ களிறு) standing at their posts.
teaches: The shared phrases show that the bard's visit to a Chera king in his foreign war camp was a set scene with its own diction, and the one change, elephants standing quiet at the post in Purananuru 22 against elephants tearing the post up in the fragment, turns the same scene from settled order to war still pending.
audit_text_issue: Fragment 4 has no colophon.

note: Kural 610 says a king without sloth (மடியிலா மன்னவன்) gains the whole earth; Fragment 4 praises a king who does not stop for the rains nor slacken for the cold (பனிஎன மடியாய்) and keeps his army in foreign land.
teaches: The Kural states freedom from sloth as a ruler's general virtue, while the fragment shows what it meant in war: refusing the seasonal halt of the rains and the cold that normally ended a campaign, so the king's tirelessness was measured against the calendar of war.

note: Both name the god by his marks, the konrai, the matted hair and the woman who is part of him; Purananuru 1 lists them without a name, Tirumanthiram 16 calls him the one whose part is the bright-browed woman.
teaches: Set beside Tirumular, the anthology's invocation shows that konrai, matted hair and the woman-part were already a fixed set of marks that identified the god without his name, and it adds what Tirumular's verse lacks: the god may also hide that female form within himself.

note: 3 ends by calling the ending of suppliants' poverty the king's true strength (வன்மை); Kural 225 ranks the strength of removing others' hunger above the strength of enduring one's own.
teaches: The Kural's ranking of strengths is abstract, and the Pandya counsel turns it into a test of practice: the giver must read the need from the face before it is spoken, and the deadly road the suppliants crossed measures what that strength owes them.

note: 5 tells the king not to side with those who cast off grace (அருள்) and love and take a hell that never leaves; Kural 243 says those whose hearts hold அருள் do not enter the dark, painful world.
teaches: The Kural makes grace a person's safeguard against hell; the Chera counsel turns the same link into a rule of government, where grace is shown by guarding the realm as one rears a child and hell is the lot of rulers who drop it.

note: Both use the weighing balance for leaning to no side: 6 wishes the king may not hold to one side, like the beam of a balance (தெரிகோல் ஞமன்ன் போல); Kural 118 makes not leaning, like a levelled scale, the ornament of the worthy.
teaches: The same balance serves as a king's blessing in the Purananuru and as a general virtue in the Kural, which shows that impartiality was pictured as a public act of weighing done by whoever judges, before it was a disposition of the private person.
audit_text_issue: purananuru:6 line 9 'ஞமன்ன்' has a doubled final consonant (ஞமன்).

note: Kural 978 says greatness always bows; 6 asks the king's umbrella and head to bow before the god's shrine and the sages, his garland to wilt only in the smoke of burned enemy lands, and his anger to yield before his women's sulking.
teaches: Where the Kural makes humility a constant trait of the great, the Purananuru poet gives it addresses: the king bows to god, sages and wives and to no one on the field, so royal humility was a question of before whom, not of always.

note: 9 praises the Pandya who, before battle, tells cows, brahmins, women, the sick and the sonless to take shelter; Kural 773 calls generous help to the foe in misfortune the cutting edge of valour.
teaches: The Kural puts mercy at the end of valour, once the foe has fallen; the Purananuru shows a king putting it before the first arrow by warning those who cannot fight, so the restraint of the brave had a set procedure as well as a maxim.

note: 10 says the Chola, seeing a proven wrong, weighs it fairly and punishes fittingly (ஒப்ப நாடி அத்தக ஒறுத்தி); Kural 561 defines a king as one who inquires fittingly and punishes in proportion (தக்காங்கு நாடி ... ஒத்தாங்கு ஒறுப்பது).
teaches: The two share the very words for inquiry and proportion, so the Kural's definition of the just king reads like a rule drawn out of praise such as this, and 10 adds what 561 leaves out: the sentence is softened for the one who comes and stands at the king's feet.

note: Kural 541 makes justice an inquiry without favour to anyone (கண்ணோடாது); 10 praises a king who lessens the penalty when the offender submits.
teaches: Read together they show that the old ideal allowed mercy after the verdict but not favour within it: the Kural bars kindly regard in the inquiry, while the Purananuru king reduces the sentence for submission, not for kinship or closeness.

note: 11 lists as glory the gold jewels and the silver-strung gold lotus a conquering Chera gave his singer and bard; 12 asks a Pandya whether giving bards gold lotuses and poets chariots is dharma when it comes from land taken to others' pain.
teaches: Side by side, the two poems show that the anthology did not take the gift economy on trust: the gold lotus that crowns the bard in 11 becomes in 12 a question about where a king's gifts come from.

note: 12 asks whether gifts made from others' land, taken so that it pains them, are dharma; Kural 659 says all that is taken with tears leaves with tears.
teaches: Nettimaiyar leaves his question to the king, and the Kural answers it with a law of return, which shows that the poet's courteous irony carries a real moral charge against the plunder that pays for the bards' gifts.

note: 14 praises the king's hands, hardened by goad, bowstring and giving, against the soft hands of his poets, which do nothing but eat; Kural 1035 honours those who eat from their own hands' work, who do not beg and who give to those who ask.
teaches: In the Kural the hand that works for its food is the hand that gives; Kapilar reverses the order and makes the poets' soft, idle hands the proof of the patron's care, so the court valued being fed as a sign of the giver's greatness where the Kural values self-support.

note: Both praise the same Pandya, Mudukudumi: 9 for warning cows, brahmins, women and the sick to shelter before battle; 15 for ploughing enemy towns with donkeys, driving chariots over their fields and bathing his elephants in their guarded tanks.
teaches: The pair shows that the righteous warning of 9 limited whom the king would kill, not what he would destroy: the same king who spares cows and the sick ploughs the enemy city into waste.

note: 16 praises a Chola for turning cool sugarcane fields into waste and feeding fire to a safe land; 18 tells a Pandya that food is land joined with water and that those who give food give life.
teaches: The anthology holds both the vanji boast of burned farmland and the counsel that farmland is life, which shows that the counsel of 18 was a duty owed to one's own land, while the enemy's fields remained a fit measure of glory.

note: 17 praises the Irumporai as lord of cool Thondi, with screwpine, wide fields, sandy groves and backwaters; Akananuru 60 compares a fisherman's guarded daughter's beauty to Thondi of the Porayan of the strong chariots.
teaches: The Poraiyan port that the praise poet counts among the king's possessions became, in akam, the standard for a girl's well-guarded beauty, which shows love poets taking their measure of value from the Chera wealth that puram poets praised.

note: Kural 542 says the whole world lives looking to the sky and the people to the ruler's sceptre; 18 says land that sows and looks to the sky (வித்திவான் நோக்கும் புன்புலம்) does not help its ruler however wide, and tells him to build tanks.
teaches: Where the Kural sets rain and the sceptre side by side as the two things people depend on, Kudapulaviyanar makes the ruler answerable for freeing the land from the sky, turning dependence on rain into a duty of public works.

note: 18 opens its argument with bodies that cannot exist without water (நீர்இன்று அமையா யாக்கை); Kural 20 says the world cannot go on without water (நீர்இன்று அமையாது உலகு).
teaches: The two share the phrase but draw different conclusions from it: the Kural derives the world's dependence on the sky, the Purananuru the king's duty to store water, so one premise supported both a praise of rain and a policy against relying on it.

note: Both name Nedunchezhiyan's victory over the seven at Alankanam (ஆலங் கானத்து; எழுவர் நல்வலம்): 19 shows the field where mothers wept and Death fled ashamed, Akananuru 36 makes the victors' shout there the measure of how loud the gossip about the hero is.
teaches: The akam poet borrowed only the victors' roar from Alankanam to measure a scandal, while the puram poem on the same battle keeps the weeping of the old houses' women, so one battle served love poetry as a byword for noise and praise poetry as a field of grief.

note: 20 ends: all living beings fear (அஞ்சும்) you; Kural 563 says a ruler who acts so as to cause dread perishes quickly. On the reading that the beings fear the king, 20 praises what the Kural condemns; on the reading that they fear for him, the two agree.
teaches: The ambiguity of 20's last line matters because the Kural's chapter against causing dread makes a feared king a doomed king, so Kurunkozhiyur Kizhar's praise only holds if the people's fear is anxiety for their ruler and not dread of him.

note: Kural 743 defines a fort by height, breadth, strength and inaccessibility; 21 describes Kanapper with a moat beyond depth, a sky-high wall and a sunless guard forest, and praises the king who took it.
teaches: The puram poet uses the full list of what makes a fort good only to measure the man who took it, so the Kural's criteria guarantee nothing to the defender: in the praise poem a perfect fort is the conqueror's ornament.

note: Both by Kalladanar to Nedunchezhiyan: 23 ends on a doe and fawn whose stag the tiger has killed; 25 ends on widows beating their breasts and shearing their hair.
teaches: The same poet states openly in 25 what 23 leaves as a bare image, which supports reading the bereaved doe of 23 as the enemy's widows and shows that a puram poet could move between the hidden and the stated forms of one grief.

note: 23 praises the victor of Alankanam; Akananuru 175 compares the lightning of the returning rains to the spear Chezhiyan raised after winning at Alankanam.
teaches: The heroine's speech in an akam poem borrows the Pandya's Alankanam victory, which 23 celebrates as fact, to measure the flashing of the rains that mark her lover's promised return, so a war became a stock image of brilliance within the poets' own generation.

note: 24 names the Mizhalai of Evvi, the generous Vel, among the lands Chezhiyan holds; Akananuru 266 names Evvi of Needur, true of sword, and the uproar after his men's victory.
teaches: One chief is remembered in the Purananuru for open-handed giving and for lands that passed to the Pandya, and in the Akananuru as a byword for the din of his war victory, so the akam poets kept a lesser king's martial name alive as a measure of loud gossip.

note: 24 ends: those who knew say the ones who truly lived are those who did not go as the many go but stood and died with lasting fame; Kural 240 says those who live without renown do not live.
teaches: The Kural's flat verdict appears in 24 as a saying the poet attributes to the wise and sets after a blessing of royal pleasure, so the maxim was already proverbial and served to bend a feast poem toward the thought of death.

note: 26 calls Chezhiyan அடுகளம் வேட்ட, the one who sacrificed the killing field; Akananuru 36 measures the town's gossip by the roar when Chezhiyan at Alankanam களம்வேட்ட, after killing seven kings in one day.
teaches: The same phrase for the battlefield sacrifice appears in a praise poem and in a heroine's quarrel with her husband, which shows the Pandya's war rite was famous enough as a phrase to serve an akam speaker as the loudest noise she could name.

note: 27 line 6 மரைஇலை போல மாய்ந்திசினோர் பலரே (many died like the lotus leaf); Naladiyar 359 ends மரையிலையின் மாய்ந்தார் பலர் (many perished like the lotus leaf).
teaches: The Naladiyar repeats the Purananuru's half-line almost word for word but moves it from nobly born kings who died without a poet's praise to people whose expectations came to nothing, and the earlier poem shows what the lotus-leaf death meant: dying without a name, beside the flower that is remembered.

note: 27 reports the saying that those whom poets praise reach a sky-car that no charioteer drives; Kural 234 says that if one wins long fame on earth, the gods' world does not honour the புலவர்.
teaches: The belief that poets' praise carries a man to heaven, which 27 gives as current hearsay, is the background the elliptical couplet assumes when it ties earthly fame to the gods' world, so the Purananuru supplies the premise the Kural leaves out.
audit_text_issue: Kural 234 sense uncertain (marker's flag).

note: 28 tells the king his wealth can achieve virtue, wealth and pleasure, and failure would be his own neglect; Kural 754 says wealth gained by right means without wrong yields virtue and pleasure.
teaches: The Kural makes the yield of virtue and pleasure depend on how wealth was gained, while the court poet makes it depend on whether the king takes care to use it, so the two books place the moral test of wealth at opposite ends, getting and spending.

note: 29 sets its blessing in a world where people pass in turn like players at a festival; Kural 332 likens wealth's coming and going to a crowd that gathers at a dance hall and disperses.
teaches: Both books reach for the festival stage to show transience, but the Purananuru applies it to the players, the people themselves, and draws the counsel to turn stored wealth into fame, while the Kural applies it to the audience, wealth itself, so the same image grounds two different lessons about what passes.
audit_text_issue: 29 is flagged uncertain; line 2 ஐது அடர்ந்ற looks misprinted.

note: 31 opens: as wealth and pleasure follow behind virtue, so the two other kings' umbrellas follow behind Nalankilli's; Kural 39 says only what comes through virtue is joy.
teaches: The ordering the Kural states as an ethical rule is used by the court poet as a ready image to rank three crowned kings, which shows the precedence of virtue over wealth and pleasure was a commonplace secure enough to carry a political claim.

note: 34 quotes dharma: there is expiation for killing cows' udders, destroying unborn children or wronging elders, but none for killing a benefit; Kural 110 says those who killed any good may escape, but not one who killed a good done to him.
teaches: The Kural compresses into a rule what the Purananuru presents as a known saying with its list of lesser crimes, and the poet turns it on himself, so the maxim was already used to bind a bard to praise his patron: gratitude here is the poet's own obligation, not only the patron's claim.

note: 35 says the king's umbrella is for sheltering his people and his victories are the fruit of the plough's furrow; Kural 1034 says those with the shade of grain-ears see many kings' umbrellas under their own king's umbrella.
teaches: Both texts set the royal umbrella against the farmer and make conquest depend on the plough, but 35 says it to the king as counsel while the Kural says it of the farmer as praise, so the same economic claim is spoken from both ends of the realm.

note: 35 says rain comes when sought in the land of the just sceptre, but also that the world blames kings for failed rains and harvests; Kural 545 says rain and harvest gather in the land of the king who rules rightly.
teaches: The Kural states the link between just rule and rain as a fact, while the court poet adds that people will blame the king for drought whatever its cause, so in the Purananuru the doctrine is also a political danger the king must manage.
audit_text_issue: Line 15 முறைவெண்டு is likely முறைவேண்டு; line 17 கொண்டுமூ is likely கொண்மூ.

note: 36 tells the besieging king that to have fought a rival who sits at ease behind his walls is a matter of shame; Naladiyar 241 says the worthy, seeing their enemies humbled, feel shame and do not advance.
teaches: The Naladiyar's maxim about shame before a humbled foe is in 36 an actual plea to stop a siege, which shows the poets used this sense of honour to bring wars to an end, and that the shame was felt to fall on the victor.

note: Both by Nappasalaiyar to Killivalavan open by naming him the descendant of the Chola who relieved a dove's distress (37 புள்ளுறு புன்கண் தீர்த்த; 39 the king who entered the scale for the dove).
teaches: The poet uses one ancestral legend of mercy in opposite ways: in 37 it heads praise of a king who spares no fine town, and in 39 it is set aside as inherited fame that cannot be his own, so the legend served both to honour the line and to ask what the living king had added.

note: 38 says heaven lacks giving and asking, so gift-seekers prefer the king's land; Kural 222 says giving is good even if there were no higher world.
teaches: Both books cut the worth of giving loose from heaven, but from opposite sides: the Kural says giving is good even without a heaven to reward it, and the Purananuru says heaven is poorer than earth because no one gives there, so giving becomes what makes this world worth more than the next.

note: 40 asks the conqueror to be sweet of speech and easy of access (இன்சொல் எண்பதத்தை); Kural 386 says the land of a king easy to see and not harsh of speech is praised above others.
teaches: The Kural's two marks of a praised king are in 40 exactly the two requests a poet puts to a victorious king, so the couplet's criteria were the counsel bards gave in person, and the poem ties them to the king's fame among his poets.

note: 41 opens 'காலனும் காலம் பார்க்கும்' (even Death watches for its time) to say the king does not wait; Naladiyar 36 tells the reader not to ask whether Death comes today or another day, for it stands right behind.
teaches: Both treat Death as an agent that chooses its hour, but the Purananuru makes that patience the measure a king exceeds, while the Naladiyar makes the unknown hour the reason for doing good now, so one belief about death supports a war boast in one book and a moral urgency in the other.

note: Kural 544: the world clings to the feet of the king who embraces his people and rules by the sceptre; 42: under his unbending sceptre the land knows no war cry, and all poets turn to him as rivers run to the sea.
teaches: The Kural states the reciprocity abstractly, while 42 shows what the embrace consists of (fields that feed guests, no raid-cry heard) and what the turning to the king looks like (poets flowing in like rivers), so the couplet's 'world at his feet' can be read as a picture of a watered, hospitable country.

note: Kural 1015 calls those who feel shame for another's fault as for their own the dwelling place of shame; in 43 the prince, wronged by the poet's words, is ashamed 'as if you had erred' (நீபிழைத் தாய்போல் நனிநா ணினையே).
teaches: The Kural's definition of the finest shame is acted out in 43 by a prince who blushes for the man who insulted him, and the poem adds the consequence the couplet omits: that shame shown this way disarms the offender, who then takes the fault on himself.

note: Kural 745 praises a fort that is hard to take, holds stored food and is easy for those inside to hold; 44 tells a besieged king that sitting secure behind shut gates and a long wall is shameful while his elephants starve and his people cry for milk and water. On the reading that both judge the king who holds out in a fort, they disagree.
teaches: The Kural values the fort as a means of holding out, while Kovur Kizhar sees the same holding out from inside, through starving beasts and infants, and calls it neither aram nor maram, so the pair shows the fort's strength and its moral cost as two views of one siege.

note: Kural 888: a house with inner enmity wears itself away like gold rubbed by a file; 45: two Cholas wearing the same aar garland fight, so whichever loses, their own house loses.
teaches: The Kural's file image says the house wears itself down, and 45 supplies the political arithmetic behind it, that between two branches of one house no outcome is a win and the only gain goes to rival dynasties, so the couplet's metaphor gets a concrete case and an outside beneficiary.

note: 45 warns two Cholas that their quarrel will give deep delight to other kings; Akananuru 346 closes on a Chola, Killi Valavan, worsted at Koodal and 'Kothai Marban's joy was great'.
teaches: An akam poet's closing allusion records exactly the outcome Kovur Kizhar predicted in puram, a rival Chera rejoicing at a Chola defeat, which shows that akam poets drew on the same remembered politics of the three crowns (whether this Killi Valavan is 45's Chola is not certain).

note: Both poems address Chola princes as descendants of the king who saved the dove (புறவு): 43 to rebuke a prince, 46 to stop the killing of children.
teaches: Placed together, the two poems show the dove story working as a family standard that poets could hold up to any Chola, in 43 to shame and in 46 to restrain, so the legend served as a check on royal conduct, not only as praise.

note: Kural 586 counsels the king to use spies who go in the guise of renunciants and wanderers; 47 insists that the bard's wandering life, crossing many wastes from patron to patron, harms no one. On the reading that 47 answers a suspicion of the wandering bard, the two disagree about whether such travellers should be trusted.
teaches: The Kural's advice to disguise spies as wanderers is the very reason a real wanderer could fall under suspicion, and 47 gives the wanderer's side, a life of gifts and honour that 'knows no harm to others', so the pair shows the cost the state's craft laid on the travelling poet.
audit_text_issue: line 4 மகழ்ந்தும் looks like a misprint for மகிழ்ந்தும்

note: 48 praises Thondi of the seaside grove, the Chera's town, as fragrant with the king's garland and the neytal of its backwater; Akananuru 60 likens the heroine's bright bangles to Thondi of Poraiyan of the strong chariot.
teaches: The same Chera port that a puram poet offers as his home and his king's glory becomes in an akam poem a measure of a girl's beauty, which shows that akam poets used a king's famous town as a byword for desirable wealth.

note: 49 asks how to name Kothai of the raised sword; Akananuru 346 ends on Kothai Marban rejoicing when a Chola was worsted at Koodal.
teaches: The Chera whom a puram poet praises as lord of three landscapes appears in akam as a rival who delights in a Chola defeat, which shows akam poets citing a living king's partisanship, not only his wealth, and lets the reader see the three-crown politics behind the praise (whether both name the same Kothai is not certain).

note: 50 says the king spared and fanned the poet as if he had heard that the higher world has a dwelling only for those with fame here; Kural 234 says that if one wins wide fame on earth the world of the gods does not honour the learned (or the gods) instead.
teaches: Both tie fame on earth to standing in the world beyond, and 50 shows the belief at work in a single act of royal mercy, while the Kural states it as a rule whose terms are disputed; the poem suggests that for a Sangam king fame was a practical reason for forbearance.

note: 51 and 52 are both poems to Maran Vazhuthi: 51 says the kings who resisted him are pitiable, living a day like winged termites; 52 shows what that pity means, their towns turning to jungle and their common hall abandoned.
teaches: Read in sequence, 51 gives the general verdict and 52 the landscape of its execution, so the reader sees how Sangam praise of a conqueror moved from a simile of brief life to a detailed picture of a deserted village.

note: Kural 1055: askers can stand before people because there are those on earth who do not hide what they have; 54: suppliants walk into the king's court 'as if they owned it' (உடையோர் போல), because he gives without stint.
teaches: The Kural explains why asking is possible at all, and 54 shows the confidence such a giver creates, a beggar entering a court with raised head; the poem also adds the other face the Kural omits, the same king's land as a tiger's ground to his rivals.

note: 55: though elephants, horses, chariots and warriors are excellent, a king's victory has the righteous way at its root; Kural 546: it is not the spear but the unbending sceptre that gives victory.
teaches: The Purananuru poet already ranks the four-limbed army below righteous rule before the Kural's couplet does, and he spells out the straight sceptre as impartiality toward one's own and others, so the Kural's maxim had a court-counsel form addressed to a named Pandya.
audit_text_issue: Line count differs from one edition (23 vs 21 lines); line 14 has stray punctuation.

note: Kural 541 defines justice as acting after inquiry without favour to anyone; 55 asks the king not to bend the rod because a man is 'ours' and not to destroy merit because he is 'others'.
teaches: The Kural forbids favour in one direction only, while 55 names both failures, favouring one's own and injuring outsiders, so the poem shows that impartiality was understood as a double duty, protecting strangers' merit as well as resisting kin.

note: 55 asks the king to be like the sun in fierce valour and like the moon in cool gentleness; 59 says the king is like the sun to his enemies and the moon to people like the poet.
teaches: The same sun-and-moon pair is counsel in 55 and description in 59, so the anthology shows a stock image of kingship moving between what a king should be and what a poet says he already is, with the second poem naming whom each face is turned to.
audit_text_issue: purananuru:55 has 23 lines against 21 in Duraisamy Pillai's edition.

note: 56 names the palmyra-bannered god and the sapphire-dark god among the four guardians of the world; 58 likens the allied Chola and Pandya to the two great gods, the milk-white one with the palmyra banner and the blue one with the wheel, standing together.
teaches: One poem divides the two gods among four to praise one king, the other pairs them to praise two allied kings, so the reader sees that poets chose a god-pair or a god-set to match the number and relation of the kings they praised.

note: 52 dwells on the enemy's land turned to jungle as the measure of the king's glory; 57 permits plunder, burning and killing in the enemy's land but asks the king to spare the guardian trees.
teaches: Set beside 52's relish of devastation, 57 shows that the same war poetry also drew a limit, and drew it at the sacred tree rather than at people, which tells us what the poets held more inviolable than the lives of the conquered.

note: 58 warns two allied kings against outsiders who come between them 'seeming good, seeming kind, seeming to follow the old ways'; Kural 826 says the words of the unreconciled, though they speak good things like friends, are soon seen through.
teaches: The Kural's general warning about feigned friendship is applied in 58 to an alliance of kings, where the danger is not the enemy's attack but his pleasant counsel, so the pair shows the couplet's subject was already a matter of statecraft.
audit_text_issue: 58 lines 6 and 7 (கிளைஅரா எறியும், அருநரை உருமின்) are obscure, as the marker notes.

note: 45 tells two quarrelling Cholas that their fight will delight other kings; 58 tells a Chola and a Pandya that if they never break their union the whole earth will be theirs.
teaches: The two poems state one calculation from opposite sides, division gives the gain to outsiders and union takes it from them, so together they show Sangam poets thinking of alliances between crowns in terms of who profits.
audit_text_issue: Purananuru 58 lines 6-7 obscure.

note: 60 likens Valavan to the strong ox that drags the salt cart's sunken wheel out of the rut on the road from the backwaters to the hill country; Akananuru 140 likens the speaker's suffering to that of the ox yoked to the father's salt cart sunk in deep mire.
teaches: The salt cart in the mire is a shared image of the coastal trade road, and the two books use opposite ends of it: the puram poet praises the king as the ox that frees the wheel, the akam speaker feels like the ox straining under it, so one working scene serves for strength in one and for heartache in the other.

note: Akananuru 55's mother, sleepless after her daughter's elopement, compares her lot to the noble men who, hearing Cheralathan's bitter words when he sat north after Venni, went with him to the other world; 65 laments the same king's sitting north (வடக்கு இருந்தனன்) out of shame at a back wound.
teaches: The akam poet can use the king's death as a simile for a mother's loss only because puram poems such as 65 had made it known, and the akam poem adds what 65 does not say: that men of his court followed him into death, so the two together give the event and its aftermath.

note: Both poems are on the death after Venni: 65 mourns the king who sat north ashamed of a back wound, and 66, addressed to the victor Karikal, says that king is better than him; both use the phrase புறப்புண் நாணி.
teaches: Read together they show the honour code reversing a battle's result: the loser's chosen death, mourned in 65 as the stopping of a whole country's life, is used in 66 to rank him above the victor, said to the victor's face.

note: Akananuru 246's friend says the gossip about the hero was louder than the uproar at Venni when Karikal broke the strength of kings and eleven Velir and their drums were left on the field.
teaches: The akam poet remembers Venni for the noise of Karikal's victory over many kings, while 66 remembers it for the defeated king's honourable death, so one battle served akam as a measure of loudness and puram as a lesson in honour.

note: Kural 970 says the world praises the radiance of those who will not live when disgrace comes; 66 says the king who sat north ashamed of his wound reached the world of great fame (மிகப் புகழ் உலகம்).
teaches: 66 shows what the Kural's general praise of honour could mean in practice: a dishonour as small as a wound's place on the body, a death chosen for it, and a poet ranking the dead man above the living victor in public.

note: The half-line எழுவர் நல்வலம் அடங்க (the strength of the seven brought down) stands in 76 line 12 and in Akananuru 36 line 20, both of Cheliyan's victory at Alankanam; Akananuru 36 names the seven kings.
teaches: The identical half-line shows that the Alankanam victory had a fixed formula that passed from praise poetry into akam, where the war-cry of that day becomes the measure of how loud the town's gossip is about the hero's new bride.

note: 76 opens: killing and being killed is not new (புதுவது அன்று), it is the way of the world; 192 says dying is not new (சாதலும் புதுவது அன்றே).
teaches: The same commonplace serves opposite ends: in 192 the oldness of death leads to calm toward great and small alike, while in 76 it is granted only so that one king's feat can stand out as the thing never heard of before.

note: In 72 the king accepts, if he breaks his vow, that his people will find no shade under his rule and will weep and blame him as cruel; Kural 555 says the tears of those who cannot bear their suffering are what wear away a king's wealth.
teaches: The Kural names the people's tears as a force that destroys a king's wealth; 72 shows a king himself choosing those tears as the worst penalty he could stake, so the Kural's warning was already a ruler's own measure of failure.

note: In 72 the kings mock Neduncheliyan as a boy (இளையன் இவன்); in 78 the new warriors say 'the fighter is young' (பொருநனும் இளையன்) and are pursued to their fathers' town and killed.
teaches: 78 tells, through a court poet, the sequel that 72 vows in the king's own voice, so the anthology keeps both the vow and its fulfilment, and the taunt of youth becomes the hinge of the king's fame.

note: 77 pictures the king as a boy just weaned, with the child's amulet still on; 72 is the same king's vow against kings who mocked him as young.
teaches: 77 shows that the enemies' taunt in 72 was literally true, which makes the boy's vow and its performance the more striking and explains why his poets kept returning to his age.
audit_text_issue: purananuru:72 line 1 'நகுதத் கனரே' is corrupt (நகுதக் கனரே).

note: Among the curses 71 accepts is to put an incapable man in office in his assembly out of fondness (அன்பின் அவையத்துத் திறன்இல் ஒருவனை நாட்டி); Kural 507 says trusting the ignorant out of fondness brings every kind of folly.
teaches: The Kural names fondness as the cause of a bad appointment; 71 shows how grave such an appointment was held to be, since a king lists it among the curses on himself beside losing his wife, his friends and his birthright.
